name: Learn: ServiceAccounts
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration & Security. Create and wire ServiceAccounts: run a pod under one, disable token automount, attach an imagePullSecret, and project a bound token. Graded exactly.
description: Five strict ServiceAccount practicals. Each Check shows which requirements you met and why any failed.

questions.title: Create a ServiceAccount
questions.teach:
A **ServiceAccount** is the identity pods use to talk to the API server. Create one with `kubectl create serviceaccount <name>`; every namespace also has a `default` SA.

**Gotcha:** pods that don't set `serviceAccountName` use `default` — give real apps their own SA for least privilege.
questions.prompt:
In `sa-learn`, create a ServiceAccount named `deployer`.

Target: ServiceAccount `deployer` exists in `sa-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n sa-learn create serviceaccount deployer
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa deployer
questions.eli5:
Imagine a Kubernetes cluster is a big office building, and the front desk (the **API server**) only lets you do things if you show a badge. People get badges — but so do the *programs* running inside, because they also need to ask the front desk for things ("list the pods", "read this config"). A program's badge is called a **ServiceAccount** (SA).

This step is just making a new badge named `deployer`, so later you can hand it to a program and say "this is who you are."

Every room in the building (every **namespace**) already comes with one generic badge called **`default`**. Any program that doesn't pick its own badge automatically wears the `default` one. That's convenient but lazy — it's like everyone sharing a single master keycard. Best practice is to give each program its *own* badge, so you can give it exactly the access it needs and nothing more (that's **least privilege**).

Making one is a one-liner: `kubectl -n sa-learn create serviceaccount deployer`.

**Watch out for:**

- **ServiceAccounts are namespaced.** A `deployer` badge in `sa-learn` is *not* the same as one in another room. Always create it in the right namespace (`-n sa-learn`).
- **Don't just rely on `default`** — real apps should get their own SA so permissions stay tight (least privilege).
- Creating the SA **does nothing by itself** — it's just an identity. It only matters once a pod uses it (next step) and RBAC rules grant it powers.
- The name must match exactly: `deployer`, lowercase, in `sa-learn`.
questions.deepDive:
## Create a ServiceAccount — full rundown

### Mental model
A **ServiceAccount (SA)** is the identity that **in-cluster workloads** (pods) use to authenticate to the **API server**. Human users authenticate with external credentials (certs, OIDC); pods authenticate as a ServiceAccount via a mounted token. An SA by itself grants **no permissions** — RBAC (Roles/RoleBindings) is what attaches powers to it.

- SAs are **namespaced** objects (`kind: ServiceAccount`, `v1`).
- Every namespace ships with a `default` SA; pods that don't name one use it.

### Create it
```bash
# imperative (simplest)
kubectl -n sa-learn create serviceaccount deployer

# declarative
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: sa-learn
YAML

# verify
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa deployer
kubectl -n sa-learn describe sa deployer
```

### What you get
| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| `metadata.name` | the SA identity (`deployer`) |
| `metadata.namespace` | SAs are namespace-scoped |
| `secrets` | in older clusters, auto-created token Secret; **empty by default** in 1.24+ |
| `imagePullSecrets` | registry creds inherited by pods using this SA (step 4) |
| `automountServiceAccountToken` | default-mount behaviour for pods (step 3) |

### Tokens: the 1.24+ change
Before Kubernetes **1.24**, creating an SA auto-created a long-lived token Secret. From 1.24 on, that stopped — pods instead get **short-lived, auto-rotated projected tokens** via the TokenRequest API. To mint a manual long-lived token:
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn create token deployer          # short-lived token to stdout
kubectl -n sa-learn create token deployer --duration=24h
```

### Granting permissions (the usual next move)
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn create role pod-reader \
  --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n sa-learn create rolebinding deployer-can-read \
  --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=sa-learn:deployer
```
Note the `namespace:name` form in `--serviceaccount`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **SAs are namespaced** — specify `-n sa-learn`; an SA in one namespace is unrelated to a same-named one elsewhere.
- **Creating an SA grants nothing** — no RBAC binding = the identity can do almost nothing.
- **Don't lean on `default`** for real apps; least privilege = dedicated SA + scoped Role.
- A pod references an SA that **doesn't exist** → the pod is rejected / stuck; the SA must exist first.
- The RBAC subject name is the **full** `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`; `--serviceaccount=ns:name` expands it for you.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn create serviceaccount deployer
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa deployer -o yaml
```

questions.title: Run a pod under a ServiceAccount
questions.teach:
Set `spec.serviceAccountName: <sa>` on a pod to run it under that identity (RBAC then applies to that SA).

**Gotcha:** it's `serviceAccountName` on the pod spec — the deprecated `serviceAccount` field still shows but don't rely on it.
questions.prompt:
In `sa-learn`, create pod `app` (image `nginx:1.25`) that runs under ServiceAccount `deployer`.

Target: pod `app`'s `serviceAccountName` is `deployer`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: app, namespace: sa-learn }
spec:
  serviceAccountName: deployer
  containers: [ { name: web, image: nginx:1.25 } ]
YAML

verification.description: pod app runs under serviceAccountName deployer

questions.eli5:
You made a badge called `deployer` in the last step. Now you actually clip it onto a program so that program *wears* that identity. The program here is a pod named `app`, and you pin the badge on by setting one field: `spec.serviceAccountName: deployer`.

Think of hiring a new worker (the pod) and telling them: *"When you talk to the front desk, use the `deployer` badge."* From then on, whatever the front desk (API server) lets the `deployer` badge do, this pod can do — and nothing more. If an admin later says "the `deployer` badge can read configs," this pod inherits that automatically. That's how **RBAC follows the identity**, not the pod.

If you *don't* set this field, the pod quietly wears the room's generic `default` badge instead.

One naming trap: the field you set is **`serviceAccountName`** (ends in "Name"). When you later look at the pod's details, Kubernetes *also* shows an older field just called `serviceAccount` — it's a leftover echo of the same value. Set the one with "Name"; don't rely on the short one.

**Watch out for:**

- **The field is `serviceAccountName`**, not `serviceAccount`. The short `serviceAccount` is deprecated and read-only-ish — set the full one.
- **It lives on the pod's `spec`** (for a Deployment, inside `spec.template.spec`), not on metadata.
- **The SA must already exist** in the same namespace, or the pod can be rejected.
- **No `serviceAccountName` = `default` SA** silently — easy to forget and then wonder why RBAC rules "don't apply."
- `serviceAccountName` is **immutable** on a running pod — recreate the pod to change it.
questions.deepDive:
## Run a pod under a ServiceAccount — full rundown

### Mental model
Setting `spec.serviceAccountName` on a pod makes that pod **authenticate to the API server as that SA**. Whatever RBAC grants the SA, the pod's processes can do (via the mounted token). This is how you give an app its own scoped identity instead of the catch-all `default`.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: sa-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: deployer     # <-- the identity
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
```

For a Deployment, the field goes in the **pod template**:
```yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: deployer
```

### Imperative shortcut
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn run app --image=nginx:1.25 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"deployer"}}'
```

### serviceAccountName vs serviceAccount
| Field | Status | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `spec.serviceAccountName` | current, canonical | **set this** |
| `spec.serviceAccount` | deprecated alias | read-only echo; don't rely on it |

After creation both show the same value in `kubectl get pod -o yaml`; the admission layer copies `serviceAccountName` into the legacy `serviceAccount`.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn get pod app -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'; echo
# deployer

# confirm the token is mounted (unless automount disabled)
kubectl -n sa-learn exec app -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
# ca.crt  namespace  token
```

### What the SA buys the pod at runtime
If automount is on (default), the pod gets:
- `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` — JWT to present to the API
- `.../ca.crt` — cluster CA to trust the API server
- `.../namespace` — the pod's namespace

RBAC bound to `deployer` then determines what calls succeed.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`serviceAccountName`, not `serviceAccount`** — the latter is deprecated; setting it won't be honored reliably.
- Field is on **`spec`** (pod) / **`spec.template.spec`** (controllers), never `metadata`.
- **SA must pre-exist** in the same namespace; a missing SA can block pod admission.
- Omitting it falls back to **`default`** silently — then your scoped RBAC "mysteriously" doesn't apply.
- **Immutable** on a live pod — delete + recreate to change the SA.
- Namespace must match: the SA is namespaced, the pod uses the SA from its **own** namespace.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn run app --image=nginx:1.25 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"deployer"}}'
kubectl -n sa-learn get pod app -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'; echo
```

questions.title: Disable token automount
questions.teach:
By default a pod gets the SA's token auto-mounted at `/var/run/secrets/...`. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (on the pod or the SA) when the app doesn't call the API — reducing blast radius if compromised.

**Gotcha:** the pod-level setting overrides the SA-level one.
questions.prompt:
In `sa-learn`, create pod `locked` (image `nginx:1.25`) with **`automountServiceAccountToken: false`**.

Target: pod `locked` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: locked, namespace: sa-learn }
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers: [ { name: web, image: nginx:1.25 } ]
YAML
questions.eli5:
By default, every pod gets handed a copy of its badge's secret **keycard** (the SA **token**), slipped into a fixed pocket inside the container at `/var/run/secrets/...`. That's handy *if* the program needs to talk to the front desk (API server). But lots of programs — like a plain web server — never call the front desk at all. Giving them a keycard they'll never use is just a liability: if a burglar breaks into that container, they find a working keycard waiting for them.

So for apps that don't need API access, you tell Kubernetes: *"don't put a keycard in this pod's pocket."* You do that with one field: `automountServiceAccountToken: false`. Smaller blast radius if the pod is ever compromised.

You can set this rule in **two places**: on the pod itself, or on the badge (the ServiceAccount) so it applies to everyone wearing it. If both say something, the **pod's** setting wins — the most specific rule beats the general one.

In this step you put it right on pod `locked`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Pod-level setting overrides the SA-level one.** If the SA says `false` but the pod says `true`, the token *is* mounted. The pod wins.
- **It's a boolean: `false`**, not the string `"false"` and not quoted in YAML in a way that makes it a string.
- Setting it `false` means **no token in the pod** — if the app later *does* need API access, it'll fail with auth errors. Only disable when the app truly doesn't call the API.
- The field sits on the **pod `spec`** (or the SA object), spelled exactly `automountServiceAccountToken`.
questions.deepDive:
## Disable token automount — full rundown

### Mental model
By default the kubelet mounts the pod's ServiceAccount **token** (plus `ca.crt` and `namespace`) into every container at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/`. If the app never calls the API server, that token is pure attack surface. `automountServiceAccountToken: false` suppresses the mount, shrinking blast radius if the pod is compromised.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: locked
  namespace: sa-learn
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # no SA token mounted
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
```

### Where you can set it + precedence
| Level | Field | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| ServiceAccount | `automountServiceAccountToken: false` | all pods using that SA (default) |
| Pod | `spec.automountServiceAccountToken: false` | just that pod |

**Pod-level overrides SA-level.** Resolution:
| SA setting | Pod setting | Result |
|---|---|---|
| unset (default true) | unset | mounted |
| `false` | unset | **not** mounted |
| `false` | `true` | mounted (pod wins) |
| `true`/unset | `false` | **not** mounted (pod wins) |

### Set it on the SA instead (fleet-wide)
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn patch serviceaccount deployer \
  -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken": false}'
```

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn get pod locked \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'; echo   # false

# prove the token dir is absent
kubectl -n sa-learn exec locked -- \
  ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount 2>&1 || echo "no token mounted"
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Pod-level wins over SA-level** — the classic exam question. Most-specific setting applies.
- **Boolean `false`, not `"false"`** — a quoted string is truthy and won't disable the mount.
- Disabling the token **breaks any in-cluster API call** the app makes (client libs auto-read that path) — only do it for apps that don't talk to the API.
- Field name is long and easy to misspell: `automountServiceAccountToken`.
- Even with automount off, you can still **explicitly** project a token via a `projected` volume (step 5) — automount only controls the *default* mount.
- Lives on the **pod spec** (or SA), not in `metadata` or on the container.

### Quick reference
```bash
# per-pod
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false

# per-SA (affects all its pods)
kubectl -n sa-learn patch sa deployer -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken":false}'

# check
kubectl -n sa-learn get pod locked -o jsonpath='{.spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'; echo
```

questions.title: Attach an imagePullSecret to the SA
questions.teach:
To pull from a private registry, create a `docker-registry` Secret and list it under the SA's `imagePullSecrets` — every pod using that SA then inherits it (no per-pod config).

**Gotcha:** `imagePullSecrets` on the **SA** applies to all its pods; on a **pod** it applies to just that pod.
questions.prompt:
In `sa-learn`, create a docker-registry Secret `regcred` (server `registry.example.com`, user `ci`, password `pass`), then add it as an **imagePullSecret** on ServiceAccount `deployer`.

Target: SA `deployer`'s `imagePullSecrets` includes `regcred`, and `regcred` is a dockerconfigjson Secret.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n sa-learn create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password=pass`, then `kubectl -n sa-learn patch serviceaccount deployer -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n sa-learn create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password=pass
kubectl -n sa-learn patch serviceaccount deployer -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
questions.eli5:
Some container images live in a **locked warehouse** (a private registry) — you can't just grab them, you need to show a key at the door. In Kubernetes, that key is a special kind of Secret called a **docker-registry secret**: it bundles the registry address, a username, and a password into the exact shape the image-puller expects.

Step one: make that key. `kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred ...` stores the warehouse address, user, and password.

Step two is the clever bit. Instead of taping the key onto every single pod by hand, you attach it to the **badge** (the ServiceAccount `deployer`) under its `imagePullSecrets` list. Now **every pod wearing that badge automatically inherits the key** — no per-pod setup. It's like giving the warehouse key to the whole department once, instead of to each worker.

Where you attach the key matters:
- On the **ServiceAccount** → all pods using that SA can pull. (what we do here)
- On a **single pod** → only that one pod can pull.

**Watch out for:**

- **The Secret must be type `docker-registry` (kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson)** — a generic Secret won't work for pulling images.
- **Patching the SA `imagePullSecrets` replaces that whole list**, so if the SA already had pull secrets, include them too or they're dropped.
- **The Secret and the SA must be in the same namespace** as the pods that use them.
- Attaching to the SA only helps **future** pods (and the pod must actually use that SA). Already-running pods created before the change don't retroactively get it.
- Registry server, username, password must be **exactly** right, or pulls fail with auth errors.
questions.deepDive:
## Attach an imagePullSecret to the SA — full rundown

### Mental model
To pull images from a **private registry**, the kubelet needs registry credentials. You store them in a `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret, then reference it via **`imagePullSecrets`**. Put it on the **ServiceAccount** and *every* pod using that SA inherits it automatically — no per-pod wiring.

### Create the registry Secret
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=ci \
  --docker-password=pass \
  --docker-email=ci@example.com      # optional
```
This produces a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` whose `.dockerconfigjson` key holds a base64 `~/.docker/config.json`.

### Attach to the ServiceAccount
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn patch serviceaccount deployer \
  -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
```
Declarative equivalent:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: sa-learn
imagePullSecrets:
- name: regcred
```

### SA-level vs pod-level imagePullSecrets
| Placed on | Field | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| ServiceAccount | `imagePullSecrets` (top level, not under `spec`) | every pod using that SA |
| Pod | `spec.imagePullSecrets` | just that pod |

Pods get the **union** of SA-level and pod-level pull secrets.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa deployer -o jsonpath='{.imagePullSecrets}'; echo
# [{"name":"regcred"}]

kubectl -n sa-learn get secret regcred -o jsonpath='{.type}'; echo
# kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson

# decode what's inside
kubectl -n sa-learn get secret regcred \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.\.dockerconfigjson}' | base64 -d; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Secret type must be `dockerconfigjson`** — made via `create secret docker-registry`. A `generic`/`Opaque` Secret won't authenticate pulls.
- **`imagePullSecrets` on the SA is a top-level field**, NOT under `spec` (SAs have no `spec`).
- **Patching replaces the whole `imagePullSecrets` array** (strategic merge treats it as a replace here) — re-include any existing entries.
- **Namespace-scoped:** Secret, SA, and consuming pods must all be in the same namespace.
- Only affects pods that **use that SA** and are **created after** the change; existing pods aren't retrofitted.
- Credentials must be exact — a wrong server/user/pass surfaces as `ImagePullBackOff` / `401 Unauthorized`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password=pass
kubectl -n sa-learn patch serviceaccount deployer \
  -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
kubectl -n sa-learn get sa deployer -o jsonpath='{.imagePullSecrets}'; echo
```

questions.title: Project a bound token
questions.teach:
A **projected `serviceAccountToken`** volume gives a pod a short-lived, **audience-scoped** token (modern workload identity) instead of the legacy long-lived secret token. Set `audience` and `expirationSeconds`.

**Gotcha:** bound tokens auto-rotate and are scoped to an audience — far safer than a static Secret token.
questions.prompt:
In `sa-learn`, create pod `token-pod` (image `nginx:1.25`, SA `deployer`) with a **projected volume** at `/var/run/secrets/tokens` containing a `serviceAccountToken` source: audience `vault`, expirationSeconds `3600`, path `token`.

Target: `token-pod` has a projected volume whose source is a serviceAccountToken with audience `vault` and expirationSeconds `3600`.
questions.hint: `volumes: [{name: tok, projected: {sources: [{serviceAccountToken: {audience: vault, expirationSeconds: 3600, path: token}}]}}]`, mounted at /var/run/secrets/tokens.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: token-pod, namespace: sa-learn }
spec:
  serviceAccountName: deployer
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    volumeMounts: [ { name: tok, mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens } ]
  volumes:
  - name: tok
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken: { audience: vault, expirationSeconds: 3600, path: token }
YAML

verification.description: token-pod projects a bound serviceAccountToken (audience vault, 3600s)

questions.eli5:
The old-style badge keycard (a long-lived Secret token) has a problem: it never expires and works for *any* door. If someone steals it, they're in forever, everywhere. The modern fix is a **one-day guest pass printed on demand**: it's valid only for a short time, auto-renews while the pod runs, and is stamped with *which building it's good for*. That stamp is the **audience**.

You give the pod this guest pass with a **projected volume**. "Projected" just means: assemble a little folder of files from live sources and mount it into the pod. Here the source is a `serviceAccountToken`, and you set:
- **`audience: vault`** — the pass only works at the door labeled "vault." Show it anywhere else and it's rejected.
- **`expirationSeconds: 3600`** — good for one hour, then Kubernetes quietly reprints a fresh one.
- **`path: token`** — name the file `token` inside the folder, mounted at `/var/run/secrets/tokens`.

So the app reads `/var/run/secrets/tokens/token`, hands it to Vault, and Vault trusts it because the audience matches.

**Watch out for:**

- **`serviceAccountToken` lives under `projected.sources`** — it's not its own volume type. Shape: `volumes: [{projected: {sources: [{serviceAccountToken: {...}}]}}]`.
- **`audience` must match what the receiver expects**, or it rejects the token. Wrong audience = denied.
- **Bound tokens auto-rotate** and are short-lived — far safer than the static legacy Secret token.
- The **`path`** is relative to the volume's mount point, giving the final file path `/var/run/secrets/tokens/token`.
- The pod should run under the right **ServiceAccount** (`deployer`) — the token represents *that* identity.
questions.deepDive:
## Project a bound token — full rundown

### Mental model
A **projected `serviceAccountToken`** volume asks the kubelet to fetch a **bound, short-lived, audience-scoped** JWT from the TokenRequest API and mount it into the pod. Unlike the legacy Secret token (long-lived, broad), a bound token:
- **expires** (and the kubelet auto-rotates it well before expiry),
- is **scoped to an audience** (only valid for the intended receiver),
- is **bound** to the pod/SA lifecycle (invalidated when the pod is deleted).

This is the modern workload-identity pattern (think Vault, cloud IAM federation).

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: token-pod
  namespace: sa-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: deployer
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tok
      mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
  volumes:
  - name: tok
    projected:
      sources:
      - serviceAccountToken:
          audience: vault
          expirationSeconds: 3600
          path: token
```
Final file path inside the container: `/var/run/secrets/tokens/token`.

### serviceAccountToken source fields
| Field | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `audience` | intended recipient of the token (`aud` claim) | defaults to the API server if omitted; receiver must match |
| `expirationSeconds` | requested lifetime | min **600** (10m); kubelet rotates at ~80% of lifetime |
| `path` | file name relative to the volume mount | required |

### Why bound beats the legacy Secret token
| | Legacy Secret token | Projected bound token |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | effectively forever | short (e.g. 1h), auto-rotated |
| Audience | API server, broad | scoped (`aud`) |
| Revocation | manual (delete Secret) | auto on pod delete / expiry |
| Storage | etcd Secret | minted on demand, in-memory tmpfs |

### Inspecting the token
```bash
kubectl -n sa-learn exec token-pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/tokens/token
# decode the payload (jwt) to see aud/exp:
kubectl -n sa-learn exec token-pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/tokens/token \
  | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null; echo
```

### Combining with other projected sources
A single `projected` volume can bundle multiple sources — token, configMap, secret, downwardAPI:
```yaml
projected:
  sources:
  - serviceAccountToken: { audience: vault, expirationSeconds: 3600, path: token }
  - configMap: { name: kube-root-ca.crt, items: [{ key: ca.crt, path: ca.crt }] }
  - downwardAPI: { items: [{ path: namespace, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.namespace } }] }
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`serviceAccountToken` is a projected *source*, not a volume type** — it must sit under `volumes[].projected.sources[]`.
- **`expirationSeconds` minimum is 600.** Request < 600 and the API bumps it up to 600; `3600` is fine.
- **`audience` must match the receiver's expectation**, or token validation fails. Default audience (omitted) is the API server itself.
- **`path` is relative** to the volume's `mountPath` — don't put a leading `/`.
- The token represents the pod's **SA identity** — set `serviceAccountName` accordingly (`deployer`).
- This works **even if `automountServiceAccountToken: false`** — projected tokens are explicit and independent of the default mount.
- Tokens are **auto-rotated by the kubelet**; apps should re-read the file, not cache the token forever.

### Quick reference
